qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says urllib3 2.0 now uses the system/OpenSSL default cipher suites. grounding_sources: urllib3 v2.0 uses system/OpenSSL configured cipher suites by default

qa_pairs.question: For SSH interoperability with pyca/cryptography's proposed ML-KEM API, is it sufficient if the library exposes the encapsulation/public key as raw bytes with no SPKI wrapper, while not exposing any serializable expanded decapsulation/private key? In my SSH use case, the client needs the ML-KEM public key as raw bytes (1184 bytes long for mlkem768x25519-sha256) plus a 32-byte X25519 public key, concatenated and sent on the wire; the server then calls encaps() on those PQ public key bytes and gets back a random secret and ciphertext, where the ciphertext is 1088 bytes and is sent back along with 32 bytes of X25519 shared data; the client then calls decaps() with its private key to recover the secret. I previously used liboqs, where whatever keypair() returned for the public key was exactly what SSH needed on the wire, and I wanted to know whether the proposed seed-only/private-key design would still work for SSH and what raw byte forms are needed.
qa_pairs.answer: The interoperability test showed that it works for SSH as needed: `public_bytes_raw()` on the public key produced exactly the bytes required on the wire, and the ciphertext returned from `encap` was also correct. The 32-byte secret was successfully exchanged in both directions. There was no need to serialize private key data, so a seed-only private-key API rather than exposing expanded private keys is not a problem for this use case.
grounding_sources: BoringSSL-backed ML-KEM support behavior (`public_bytes_raw()` output and `encap` ciphertext)

title: Handle links and other safe content inside translations

qa_pairs.question: In Rails translations, is there a built-in way for `t`/rails-i18n to preserve `SafeBuffer` when interpolating HTML-safe values, so I can write: ```yml text: some <> text with an %{insert} text_html: some <> text with an %{insert} insert: a link, properly escaping <> ``` and then render: ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` without needing either of these workarounds: ```erb <%= t(".text", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)).html_safe %> ``` or ```erb <%= t(".text_html", insert: link_to(t(".insert"), root_path)) %> ``` The goal is that the translation key should not need to know whether `insert` contains HTML, and that `link_to` returning an `html_safe` string would produce: ```html some <> text with an a link, properly escaping <> ``` The Rails i18n guide does not mention a nice way to do this; can Rails handle this automatically by being aware of `SafeBuffer`?
qa_pairs.answer: A maintainer replied that they had just implemented a version of this behavior themselves and shared a gist with their approach. They said they would love for something like that to become part of Rails or rails-i18n, but did not point to any existing built-in Rails support.

title: remove prepare script using husky and deprecated husky set from npm package

qa_pairs.question:
When installing axios@1.9.0 as a transitive dependency in a monorepo, npm fails with:
```\nnpm error .git can't be found\nnpm error > axios@1.9.0 prepare:hooks\nnpm error > npx husky set .husky/commit-msg "npx commitlint --edit $1"\nnpm error husky - install command is DEPRECATED\n```
The published package appears to include these scripts:
`"scripts": {
  "prepare": "husky install && npm run prepare:hooks",
  "prepare:hooks": "npx husky set .husky/commit-msg \"npx commitlint --edit $1\""
}`
This breaks consumer installs because it assumes a `.git` directory exists, uses deprecated Husky commands (`install`, `set`), and runs developer-only tooling during install. Can axios remove the prepare script from the published package or otherwise change the Husky setup so axios 1.9.0 can install as a transitive dependency in monorepos/CI without failing?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says they created PR #6944 to switch to `postinstall` with safely guarded Husky install scripts so installation will not fail when there is no `.git` directory. They also say they intend to keep hook setup automatic for contributors instead of moving it to a manual `husky:init` command.

title: README beforeRedirect example bypasses follow-redirects credential-stripping protection

qa_pairs.answer: Yes. The maintainer agreed the README example should check that the redirect is still HTTPS before re-injecting credentials, for example by checking `new URL(redirectUrl).protocol === 'https:'`, and said the docs should note that `follow-redirects` intentionally strips credentials on HTTPS→HTTP downgrades and that `beforeRedirect` runs after that stripping.

title: Stripe.PaymentIntent type is incompatible with stripe-js version of PaymentIntent

qa_pairs.question:
I'm creating a PaymentIntent on the server with stripe-node, and I originally tried to return a reduced version of the server-side `Stripe.PaymentIntent` to the client as an `@stripe/stripe-js` `PaymentIntent`. I hit type incompatibilities such as:

```
Type 'import("stripe").Stripe.PaymentIntent.LastPaymentError' is not assignable to type 'import("@stripe/stripe-js").PaymentIntent.LastPaymentError'.
  The types of 'payment_method.customer' are incompatible between these types.
    Type 'string | Customer' is not assignable to type 'string'.
      Type 'Customer' is not assignable to type 'string'.ts(2322)
```

and:

```
Type 'string | PaymentMethod' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  Type 'PaymentMethod' is not assignable to type 'string'.ts(2322)
```

My reducer looked like this:

```ts
import { PaymentIntent } from '@stripe/stripe-js'
import Stripe from 'stripe'

// pi parameter should be of Stripe.PaymentIntent type - the server side PaymentIntent type definition
// But Stripe.PaymentIntent is incompatible with @stripe/stripe-js version of PaymentIntent.
// The below code results in Typescript error.

function reduceStripePIToPublishableKeyPermissions(pi: Stripe.PaymentIntent): PaymentIntent {
    return {
        id: pi.id,
        amount: pi.amount,
        client_secret: pi.client_secret,
        currency: pi.currency,
        description: pi.description,
        last_payment_error: pi.last_payment_error,
        next_action: pi.next_action,
        payment_method: pi.payment_method,
        payment_method_types: pi.payment_method_types,
        receipt_email: pi.receipt_email,
        setup_future_usage: pi.setup_future_usage,
        shipping: pi.shipping,
        status: pi.status,
        object: pi.object,
        canceled_at: pi.canceled_at,
        cancellation_reason: pi.cancellation_reason,
        capture_method: pi.capture_method,
        confirmation_method: pi.confirmation_method,
        created: pi.created,
        livemode: pi.livemode
    }
}
```

After reading more, it seems the frontend often only needs the `client_secret`, but I wanted to use the PaymentIntent as a single source of truth so the UI amount/currency matches what will actually be charged. In this case, is Stripe's preferred approach to pass only the `client_secret` from the server and then have the client query Stripe as needed? Also, is there any built-in redaction function in `stripe-node` for converting a server-side PaymentIntent into a publishable-key-safe object?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says there is no built-in redaction in `stripe-node`, and they would not add one for now. They say you could retrieve the PaymentIntent server-side with the publishable key, but that is effectively the same as retrieving it client-side after passing back the `client_secret`. For passing extra display data like amount or currency, they recommend sending your own separate object between your server and client.

title: Vulnerable dependency version that is 12 years old: path-to-regexp

qa_pairs.question:
In Express 4.22.1 on all platforms (Node.js 22.x, though that seems irrelevant), `npm audit` reports a vulnerable `path-to-regexp` dependency and the package appears to be 12–13 years old according to these pages:
- https://security.snyk.io/package/npm/path-to-regexp
- https://www.npmjs.com/package/path-to-regexp?activeTab=versions

Is Express 4.22.1 actually using a vulnerable `path-to-regexp`, and if not, what version should be installed and what should I do if an older version is present?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says Express 4.22.1 depends on `path-to-regexp` as `~0.1.12`, which should resolve to `0.1.13`, and that `0.1.13` is not known to be affected by vulnerabilities per the Snyk page. If an older version is installed, they advise running `npm update path-to-regexp` or `npm audit fix`; a fresh install without `node_modules` should also install `path-to-regexp@0.1.13`.
